::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
**Question 4.1** (based on section 4.1–4.3)

Replacing incandescent bulbs with LED lamps is an example of which strategy?

a) Efficiency
b) Consistency
c) Sufficiency

**Question 4.2** (based on section 4.1–4.3)

Switching from fossil fuels to solar, wind and hydropower is an example of which strategy?

a) Efficiency
b) Consistency
c) Sufficiency

**Question 4.3** (based on section 4.1–4.3)

Reducing working time in order to lower production and resource use is an example of which strategy?

a) Efficiency
b) Consistency
c) Sufficiency

**Question 4.4** (based on section 4.1–4.3)

Which strategy focuses mainly on the consumption side rather than the production side?

a) Efficiency
b) Consistency
c) Sufficiency

**Question 4.5** (based on section 4.1)

What is the main criticism of relying on the efficiency strategy alone?

a) It is too expensive for companies
b) Rebound effects can reduce or even cancel out the savings from efficiency gains
c) It requires people to give up their standard of living
d) It only works for renewable energy

**Question 4.6** (based on section 4.2)

With today’s best technology, material cycles can be fully closed without any losses of mass or energy.

a) True
b) False

**Question 4.7** (based on section 4 (Introduction))

What does the script conclude about the three strategies?

a) Efficiency alone will be sufficient if technology advances fast enough
b) Consistency should replace the other two strategies
c) Achieving the sustainability goals probably requires all three strategies working together
d) Sufficiency is the only strategy that really works

#### Answers and explanations {.unnumbered}

**4.1** a). Efficiency means using fewer resources and less energy for the same output. LEDs provide the same light with less electricity. The strategy starts on the production side and relies mainly on technological progress.

**4.2** b). Consistency (eco-effectiveness) seeks compatibility between technology and natural cycles rather than simply using less. Renewable energy works with natural rhythms instead of consuming fossil stocks. Electronics designed for repair and recycling (“cradle to cradle”) are another example.

**4.3** c). Sufficiency asks how much we need for a good life and aims to reduce demand for resource-intensive goods and services. It can be practised by individuals (sharing instead of buying), companies (sufficiency-oriented product design) and governments (sufficiency policy, such as working-time reduction).

**4.4** c). Efficiency and consistency both start on the production side. Sufficiency focuses on consumption and needs, though not exclusively.

**4.5** b). Efficiency gains often make goods and services cheaper, which can increase demand (see Chapter 3.1.3). Critics therefore warn against overestimating the effect of efficiency on absolute resource use.

**4.6** False. False. Material cycles always involve losses of mass and energy, and even fully biodegradable products need energy to produce. Absolute consistency is an unattainable ideal, but it still serves as a target for reducing resource use and emissions as far as possible.

**4.7** c). Practically all approaches to sustainable development build on the three strategies, but they weigh and prioritize them differently. The script’s conclusion is that the goals will probably only be achieved if all three work together.

:::
